Protect corridors and sites

Encroachment surveys for concessions, sites and boundaries

A concession, estate or project site is only as secure as its edge. We map the structures inside your boundary, in a ring around it, or both, list each one with its position and distance to the boundary, and compare the edge between dated surveys for new structures, cleared ground and tracks. You see where land is being occupied, and decide what happens next.

Used in: Mining · Renewables · Agriculture, forestry & nature

Request a proposal How we detect and review

What it is

What stands inside and around your boundary

Boundaries are long and rarely walked. A mining right, an exploration licence, a plantation, a solar site or a special economic zone can run for tens of kilometres of edge, most of it out of sight of the gate. Settlement pressure builds from outside: new homesteads at the edge, fields cleared across the line, a track opened to reach them. Inside, structures can appear on land you need for an expansion or a buffer.

An encroachment survey records the position of each structure against your boundary, inside, outside or both, so your tenure, land and social-performance teams can see the pattern and engage early. It uses the same method as our right-of-way surveys, applied to a polygon instead of a line.

The same register works for industrial estates, ports, free zones and land banks, where the question is what has been built on land held for a purpose.

Words we use, and don’t

We describe structures, cleared ground, excavations and tracks, never the people who built them, and we never label a structure illegal. What the imagery shows is a fact. Its status is your decision and the authorities’.

How it works

Three ways to survey a boundary

Your land

Inside the boundary

The structures inside the concession, site or estate, with an optional setback so structures close to the edge are listed separately. Useful before an expansion, a resettlement or a handover.

The approach

In a ring around it

The structures within a ring of the width you choose outside the boundary, where settlement pressure usually builds first. Each structure is listed with its distance to the edge.

Change at the edge

Both, compared over time

Inside and outside together, re-surveyed on a schedule agreed with you. New structures, cleared ground and new tracks at the edge are flagged and confirmed by a reviewer.

  1. Boundary and bands

    You send the polygon and we agree the ring width, any inside setback, and the zones inside the boundary that matter most, such as a planned pit, a buffer or a conservation set-aside.

  2. Structures and categories

    We map structures from dated imagery and open building datasets; reviewers confirm them, mark by hand where automatic detection is not enough, and, where scoped, tag each with what the imagery shows: main building, outbuilding, livestock enclosure, under construction.

  3. Edges, tracks and fences

    New tracks and access roads into the area are mapped between dates. Fence lines and gates are checked by a reviewer on drone orthophotos, subject to the approvals and security clearances each flight requires.

  4. Review and delivery

    A person reviews every result. You receive the register, maps and GIS layers, and a notice after each re-survey.

What you receive

A boundary register and the layers behind it

  • A structure register with ID, coordinates, inside or outside, distance to the boundary and, where scoped, a reviewer category
  • Area figures: the area surveyed and the structures inside and within each band of the boundary
  • An area-wide structure layer for large concessions and districts, ready for your own GIS
  • Boundary change between dated surveys: new structures, cleared ground and new tracks at the edge
  • A PDF report in English or Portuguese, GIS layers (GeoPackage, GeoJSON, KMZ, Shapefile) and an interactive map file

The services behind it

Every proposal names the services it includes. These are the ones this solution draws on.

Encroachment and structure mapping

  • Concession, site and boundary encroachment surveyStructures inside your concession, site or land-use boundary, in a ring around it, or both, mapped and listed so you can see where land is being occupied.
  • Area-wide structure mappingA GIS layer of structures across a whole district, concession or imagery survey, ready to load into your own mapping system.
  • Reviewer-led structure mappingWhere automatic detection is not enough, such as dense villages, mixed tree cover or unusual roofs, AfriScan reviewers mark structures by hand on high-resolution imagery.
  • Structure categories and attributesA reviewer tags each structure with what the imagery shows, such as main building, outbuilding, livestock enclosure, under construction or roof type, for resettlement and planning registers.

Change and repeat surveys

  • Boundary and perimeter changeNew structures, cleared ground and new tracks at your boundaries between dates, with fence lines and gates checked by a reviewer on drone imagery.

Detection of specific features

  • Track and access-route mappingNew tracks and access roads into your concession, across your right of way or around your site, mapped between dates.

Limits

What an encroachment survey is not

What it shows

  • Where structures stand relative to your boundary, and how that changes between dated surveys
  • Where land is being cleared or opened up with new tracks
  • What the imagery shows about each structure, where categories are scoped

What it does not show

  • Whether a structure is authorised, or who built or uses it
  • Title, tenure or the legal line of your boundary
  • Structures under dense canopy, and fences on satellite imagery
  • Anything about people: we map land and assets, never who is on them

Who uses it

Holders of concessions, estates and sites

Mining

Tenure and social-performance teams watching concession and mining-right edges, land needed for expansions, and the approaches to haul roads and plants.

Concession edges

Renewables

Sites and connection lines

Agriculture, forestry & nature

Estate and plantation managers, conservation areas and offset sites tracking structures, clearing and new tracks at their boundaries.

Estates and plantations

Also used for well pads, plant perimeters and LNG host areas and their corridors, substation sites, and public land held by government and development agencies.

Frequently asked questions

Will you tell us whether a structure is illegal?

No. We map what is on the land and where it sits relative to your boundary. Whether a structure is authorised, and what to do about it, is for you and the authorities to decide.

Can you confirm our title or land-use right?

No. We measure against the boundary you supply, such as a concession limit, a lease or a Mozambican DUAT boundary. We do not verify title, tenure or where a boundary legally runs; that is work for a registered land surveyor or the cadastre.

Can you check fences and gates?

Yes, on drone imagery. Fence lines are too thin to detect reliably on satellite imagery, so a reviewer checks them on drone orthophotos of the stretches you choose, subject to the approvals and security clearances each flight requires.

Our concession is very large. Is that a problem?

No. Large areas are delivered as a structure layer across the whole concession, with detailed registers and reviewer categories for the edges, the ring and any zones you choose. The proposal sets out which imagery covers which part.

Does this cover people moving onto the land?

We map structures, cleared ground and tracks, not people. The survey shows where land is being built on or cleared; it never identifies who is there.

Send us the boundary you are answerable for.

A concession, lease, estate or site polygon as KML, KMZ, GeoJSON, Shapefile or GeoPackage, and the ring width you want to watch. We reply with a written proposal.
